author: Nick Hanson
title: Building the Cosmic Database: A Final Project Journey
excerpt:
What started as a class project became something much bigger—a story-building app for a galaxy I’ve been dreaming up.
The Cosmic Database is part web app, part writing tool, and part crash course in object-oriented PHP, database design,
and just barely beating the deadline. This is the story of how I built it, broke it, fixed it, and learned more than I
expected along the way.
content:
For my PHP & MySQL final project, I decided to do more than just meet the minimum requirements. I wanted to build
something I could actually use and expand upon beyond the class. So I created the Cosmic Database: a full-featured,
multi-module web application to manage alien species, characters, and worldbuilding elements for a sci-fi story I’m
developing with my son and some others.
This blog reflects the chaotic (but rewarding) process of building, breaking, debugging, deploying, and polishing a
full-stack PHP project on both Windows and Linux environments. Spoiler alert: it got done. Barely.

The Goal
The vision for the Cosmic Database was a story-building tool: something that could handle not just species and characters,
but eventually planets, ships, and factions too. But for Phase 1, I narrowed it to:
Add/edit/delete species and characters
Associate characters with species (many-to-many via a junction table)
User login/signup system with admin/user roles
Admin-only deletion/edit permissions
Profile editing (name, username, password, profile pic)
Sticky header/footer and styled interface via Bootstrap
Full object-oriented backend using PHP classes

The Stack
PHP (OOP)
MySQL (via mysqli with prepared statements)
Apache (XAMPP locally, then deployed to Linux server)
Bootstrap for UI
Sessions for access control

Highlights (and Hiccups)
✅ Object-Oriented Refactor
After the base version was working, I refactored species and characters into full PHP classes, complete with:
Private properties
Getters and setters
insert(), queryAll(), and display methods
This not only made things cleaner, but modular enough to scale in the future.

🛠️ Hidden Gotchas
Session issues: Clicking links worked fine locally, but failed silently on the Linux server due to misconfigured $_GET
params and session_start() being too late.
Pathing madness: __DIR__ and file system paths worked locally but failed on Linux until I switched to clean web paths
(e.g., /projects/project4/images/...)
Foreign key constraints: Attempting to delete characters before clearing junction table entries caused FK constraint
failures until I added a proper cascade or manual delete-first logic.
Password fields: Pre-filling password fields caused passwords don’t match errors until I stripped the value attribute
entirely. Rookie mistake.

🎯 Last-Minute Polish
Added a sticky footer with a logout link for clean UX
Cleaned up the navmenu to show/hide links based on user access level
Made sure delete icons (trash cans) only show for admins
Implemented file upload limits and basic image validation

Deployment Panic
The app was due by midnight. I deployed to the required Linux server around 3:30am. Everything mostly worked, except for
broken paths, FK issues, and profile image loading failing due to file permission errors.
Did I submit late? Yeah. Did I email my instructor a quick heads-up and hope for mercy? Also yes.

Final Thoughts
This project pushed every single skill I learned in the course: from handling SQL joins and secure form input, to using
sessions, and writing real object-oriented PHP. But more than that, I got to build something I care about—a tool that ties
into a creative project I want to keep working on.
Would I do it again? In a heartbeat. But maybe next time I’ll submit before 3:30am.

Bonus Lesson:
If you're ever 99% sure your URL param is correct... check anyway. It’s always the 1% assumption that breaks everything.

Thanks for following the journey!

Nick HansonWeb Software Developer
